title: Implant Burns Off Excess Blood Sugar Without Insulin or Drugs in Mouse Study
excerpt: An ETH Zurich team led by Martin Fussenegger, with Debasis Maity as first author, built a wireless catalyst implant that converts blood glucose to gluconate — controlling sugar within an hour in diabetic mice, with human tests still ahead.
body:
• Researchers at ETH Zurich, in a study published in Science and led on the bench by first author Debasis Maity, have built an implant that removes excess glucose from blood using an electrically powered catalyst — no insulin, no drugs, no living cells.
  • In diabetic mice with obesity, the device brought blood sugar under control within an hour of switching on and held it there over six weeks; the mice also lost weight and showed lower triglycerides.
  • Reader reality check: this has never been tested in humans. There is no human efficacy or risk data yet — in percentage terms, the proven benefit today is in mice over six weeks, not in people at all — so no one should change diabetes medication on the basis of this study.
  • The closed-loop design pairs a standard arm-worn glucose sensor with a smartphone, which switches the implant on only when glucose rises too high and off again when it falls.

An implant about the size of a USB stick can pull excess sugar directly out of the blood, without insulin or any other drug, researchers at ETH Zurich have shown in a study published in Science. The device, called ECHO — electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization — was developed by a team led by Professor Martin Fussenegger, with Debasis Maity as first author of the paper. According to ETH Zurich, the system is a potential new approach to type 2 diabetes, a condition in which the problem is often a chronic surplus of energy that insulin alone does not address: insulin moves glucose into cells, but unused energy is still stored as fat, which is why many patients keep gaining weight on treatment.

How the implant works

Earlier attempts by the same group used genetically engineered cells to regulate blood sugar. Those biological systems raised problems with immune tolerance, stability, manufacturing and regulatory approval. ECHO abandons biology entirely. Its catalyst is made only from inorganic materials: graphite felt studded with gold nanoclusters decorated with still smaller platinum particles, housed with an electronic control unit in a 3D-printed casing and powered wirelessly at 13.56 MHz, a frequency reserved internationally for medical applications.

When voltage is applied, the catalyst's surface oxidises glucose into gluconate, a metabolite the body can process easily. Scientific American reported that in the mouse experiments about a fifth of the resulting gluconate was burned for energy and the rest was flushed out through the kidneys — glucose that is therefore never stored as fat. Remarkably, the catalyst targeted glucose specifically among similar blood sugars such as fructose and galactose, an effect Fussenegger told Scientific American the team cannot yet explain: "The specificity is, I would say, a lucky strike."

"For decades, we have treated diabetes by telling the body how to manage glucose. We are now showing that we can take control of glucose directly, using electronics rather than drugs."

— Martin Fussenegger, ETH Zurich

What the mouse results do — and do not — show

In diabetic mice with obesity, the implant brought blood glucose under control within an hour of being switched on, and repeated treatment held it there for six weeks, Scientific American reported. The mice showed reduced triglycerides and lower body weight. ETH Zurich said removed implants still worked after six weeks, tissue showed no signs of inflammation or scarring in the study, and the system ran at very low voltage with no evidence of tissue damage from electrical or thermal effects. In a separate bench test, the catalyst also converted glucose in five litres of solution — roughly the volume of blood in a human body.

The limits are equally clear, and they matter for the large number of diaspora readers managing type 2 diabetes. The team has not tested the device on humans. Six weeks of stability in mice says nothing yet about years of use in a person, long-term tissue compatibility, or whether catalytic activity holds at human scale outside a flask. Independent chemist Luisa Torsi of the University of Bari, who was not involved in the study, told Scientific American that six weeks of operational stability is "already well beyond the current technology," but that the crucial next steps are long-term compatibility and safe, effective glucose removal at human scale.

What happens next

The team now plans to develop the system into a medical device. Because the glucose-lowering mechanism uses no cells or enzymes, and the external parts — glucose sensors, wireless power, phone-based control — are already commercially available, the researchers argue development could be more straightforward than for cell-based implants. That is a researcher's hope, not a timeline: human trials, regulatory review and long-term safety data all stand between this mouse study and any clinic.
